text: Cassini launched on 15 October 1997 from Cape Canaveral, riding a Titan IVB/Centaur rocket.
Cassini-Huygens was the largest interplanetary spacecraft ever built: 6.7 m high, more than 4 m wide and 5.6 tonnes at launch.
Too heavy to fly straight to Saturn, Cassini swung past Venus twice (1998 and 1999), Earth (August 1999) and Jupiter (December 2000) to pick up speed.
Cassini became the first spacecraft to orbit Saturn on 1 July 2004 UTC, which was still 30 June at its home base in California.
To slow into orbit around Saturn, Cassini fired its main engine for 96 minutes.
Cassini ran on three radioisotope thermoelectric generators, which turn the heat of decaying plutonium-238 into electricity.
On 14 January 2005 the Huygens probe landed on Titan: the first, and so far only, landing on any world in the outer solar system.
The battery-powered Huygens probe kept working for another 72 minutes on the surface of Titan.
In July 2005 Cassini's cameras caught water vapour and ice spraying from warm fractures at the south pole of the small moon Enceladus.
Cassini found large lakes of liquid hydrocarbons in Titan's northern latitudes, and seas of liquid methane.
Cassini made the highest-resolution movie yet of the hexagon, a six-sided jet stream around Saturn's north pole.
The orbiter carried 12 science instruments and the Huygens probe carried six.
The pictures here come from Cassini's Imaging Science Subsystem: a narrow-angle and a wide-angle digital camera, the NAC and WAC windows.
On 19 July 2013 Cassini slipped into Saturn's shadow and photographed the planet, seven of its moons, its inner rings and Earth: "The Day Earth Smiled".

The mission is named after two astronomers: Giovanni Domenico Cassini, who found Iapetus, Rhea, Tethys and Dione and the Cassini Division in the rings, and Christiaan Huygens, who discovered Titan in 1655.
Cassini-Huygens was a joint mission of NASA, the European Space Agency and the Italian space agency ASI.
Cassini discovered new moons of Saturn, among them Methone and Pallene in 2004, Daphnis, Anthe and Aegaeon.
The Equinox extension alone added 60 orbits of Saturn, 26 flybys of Titan and seven of Enceladus.
In its Grand Finale, starting April 2017, Cassini made 22 orbits that each passed through the gap between Saturn and its rings.
On 15 September 2017 Cassini was deliberately plunged into Saturn's atmosphere, so it could never crash into and contaminate Enceladus or Titan.
Cassini's last signal was received at 4:55 a.m. PDT on 15 September 2017 by NASA's Deep Space Network antennas in Canberra, Australia.
